entries.title: Complaints Against DOJ Officials Have Surged During Trump’s Second Term
entries.summary: The Office of Professional Responsibility has seen a 54% increase in misconduct complaints over the last two years, an inspector general report found.
entries.content:
Professional misconduct complaints against Department of Justice personnel have surged during President Donald Trump’s second term, according to an annual inspector general report documenting the department’s top challenges.

Tuesday’s findings from the department’s independent oversight office follow last year’s workforce reductions and a record-high caseload that includes dozens of lawsuits against the president’s political opponents.

The high number of complaints have led the department to open investigations into attorney misconduct, whistleblower retaliation and federal law enforcement conduct violations, the report says.

The DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility reported receiving 2,081 professional misconduct complaints last fiscal year, representing a 54% increase from 1,346 in 2024, the last full fiscal year during then-President Joe Biden’s administration, the report says.

The administration has been quickly outpacing DOJ complaints filed during Biden’s tenure, which were at their lowest in fiscal year 2023 at 1,085 recorded complaints, and their highest in 2024.

OPR found professional misconduct in each of the nine full-scale investigations that it completed this year, while one additional investigation has not yet been concluded, the report says. The office also received 50 new FBI whistleblower retaliation complaints.

The inspector general noted that the surge in misconduct complaints has put strain on the department’s shrinking workforce.

“These results demonstrate that OPR has continued to resolve substantial workloads despite its limited size,” the report states. “However, the Department faces risk in its oversight capacity if OPR’s staffing levels are insufficient to manage the workload generated by the Department’s thousands of employees.”

The review coincides with a record number of staff departures at the Department of Justice. The report cites a net decline of 10,345 department employees between January 2025 and May 2026.

Staffing levels are also impacting federal prosecutors’ ability to try cases across the country.

The report acknowledged concerns over the loss of critical expertise across the department, noting a 40% vacancy rate in the Missing or Murdered Indigenous Persons Regional Outreach Program and sprawling staffing issues in the Bureau of Prisons.

“Workforce reductions may produce mission degradation that aggregate staffing numbers do not reveal, particularly where departures are concentrated in specialized or difficult-to-replace positions,” the report warned.
